description: John Ball, the Poll Tax and the cost of war combined to bring England to the brink of revolt.
content_html:
Why 1381? Building Towards Revolt

The Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 did not erupt from nowhere. It was the product of decades of accumulated grievances stretching back to the Black Death and even earlier — combined with a specific set of short-term triggers in the late 1370s and early 1380s. Understanding both the long-term causes (the structural injustices of medieval English society) and the short-term catalysts (the Poll Tax, the French Wars) is essential for analysing why this particular moment produced revolt.

Long-Term Causes: The Issue of Serfdom

At the core of the revolt was the continued existence of serfdom. As explored in the previous lesson, the Black Death had created a labour shortage that gave surviving peasants real economic leverage. Many expected that the practical decline of serfdom would be formalised — that they would be freed from their legal obligations to their lords. Instead, the Statute of Labourers (1351) tried to restore the pre-plague order and keep wages down.

Over the following three decades, the tension between peasants who felt they had earned their freedom through their indispensable labour and lords who used the courts to enforce serfdom built steadily. Manorial court records from the 1360s and 1370s show increasing numbers of cases where lords prosecuted peasants for leaving their manors or refusing to perform labour obligations. This legal pressure was a constant source of resentment.

Key Fact

The long-term causes of the Peasants’ Revolt included the continued enforcement of serfdom after the Black Death, the Statute of Labourers (1351) attempting to reverse wage gains, and decades of resentment at the gap between peasants’ economic reality and their legal status as unfree servants of their lords.

The Religious Ideas of John Ball

One of the most influential voices of peasant discontent was John Ball. Ball was a wandering priest who had been repeatedly imprisoned for preaching without licence. His message was simple and explosive: God made all people equal; serfdom was therefore not divinely ordained but a human invention imposed by the rich to exploit the poor.

Ball’s most famous expression of this idea was his rhyme: “When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?” — arguing that at the beginning of the world there were no lords and no serfs, only working people. This egalitarian message resonated deeply with peasants who had seen their practical importance to the economy grow while their legal status remained that of property. Ball was in prison at the time of the revolt but was broken out by the rebels, becoming one of its leading voices.

Ball’s ideas intersected with a broader religious ferment in late fourteenth-century England. The theologian John Wyclif (c. 1328–1384) was developing critiques of the Church’s wealth and authority that would later inspire the Lollards. While Wyclif himself was a university theologian and not directly connected to the revolt, the wider climate of questioning Church authority — especially the wealth and worldliness of senior clergy — fed into the atmosphere of discontent that produced 1381.

The Cost of the French Wars

By the late 1370s, the Hundred Years’ War had turned dramatically against England. The gains of the Treaty of Brétigny (1360) had been steadily eroded by French counter-attacks under Charles V. English armies were being driven out of territory won in the previous generation, and the cost of military campaigns was enormous. The Crown needed money, and it needed it fast.

The ordinary taxation of the period fell heavily on the poorest. Parliamentary subsidies, which funded the wars, were assessed on moveable goods — meaning peasants who owned some property paid, while the very poorest contributed nothing and the very richest paid proportionally less than their wealth warranted. The wars drained resources from communities already struggling, and the lack of decisive military victory made the taxation feel like exploitation without return.

Key Fact

The failing French Wars of the late 1370s created a fiscal crisis. Parliament imposed three Poll Taxes between 1377 and 1381 to fund military campaigns. The third Poll Tax of 1380 — collected in 1381 — was set at one shilling per head for every person over fifteen, regardless of wealth, and its deeply unfair flat rate was the immediate trigger for revolt.

The Poll Taxes of 1377-1381

Three Poll Taxes were levied between 1377 and 1381 to fund the French Wars. The first two were less resented because they were graduated — the wealthy paid more. The third Poll Tax, passed in 1380 and collected in early 1381, was deeply different: it imposed a flat rate of one shilling on every person over fifteen. For a lord, one shilling was trivial; for a peasant family, it could represent a week’s wages. Many communities simply refused to pay or hid people from tax collectors.

When the government sent out commissioners to investigate evasion and collect the unpaid tax in 1381, the result was explosive. In Essex and Kent — areas where the Statute of Labourers had been especially aggressively enforced — the arrival of tax commissioners became the final spark.

The Role of Wat Tyler

Wat Tyler emerged as the leading figure of the Kentish rebels in 1381. His exact background is uncertain, but he proved an effective military organiser, leading the march on London and negotiating with Richard II at Mile End. Tyler represented the convergence of specific short-term grievances — the Poll Tax, the French Wars’ failures — with the deeper, longer-term anger about serfdom and inequality that John Ball had given intellectual expression.

The Peasants’ Revolt began in Essex and Kent for specific reasons. Both counties had experienced aggressive enforcement of the Statute of Labourers. Both had relatively prosperous peasant communities with enough resources to organise resistance. Essex was close to the legal records and institutions the rebels targeted in London; Kent was the route through which French raids had recently threatened the coast, making taxation for failed wars especially bitter. The arrival of Poll Tax commissioners in these specific counties acted as the detonator for grievances that had been accumulating for decades.
exam_tip_html: Examiners expect you to distinguish between long-term and short-term causes of the Peasants’ Revolt. Long-term: serfdom, the Statute of Labourers (1351), the Black Death’s economic legacy. Short-term: the Poll Taxes (especially 1380), the failing French Wars, the arrival of tax commissioners in 1381. For a “how far do you agree” question about causes, you must weigh these against each other — not just list them. Always link John Ball’s ideas to the wider context of serfdom and the Black Death’s legacy, not just to the revolt itself.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Long-term causes of the Peasants’ Revolt included the continued legal enforcement of serfdom after the Black Death, the resentment created by the Statute of Labourers (1351), and decades of tension between peasants’ economic value and their legal status.
  • John Ball’s radical preaching argued that God made all people equal and serfdom was contrary to divine law; his ideas gave intellectual expression to peasant resentment and helped inspire the revolt.
  • The short-term triggers were the failing French Wars, which demanded heavy taxation, and the flat-rate Poll Tax of 1380/1381, which imposed a shilling per head regardless of wealth — sparking revolt in Essex and Kent when commissioners tried to collect unpaid amounts.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of John Ball's religious ideas.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for a simple identification, 2 for a developed feature. Example: John Ball preached that God made all people equal [1]; he argued that serfdom was therefore not divinely ordained but a human invention used by the rich to exploit the poor, expressed in his rhyme 'When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?' [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Poll Tax of 1380.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Feature 1: The 1380 Poll Tax imposed a flat rate of one shilling on every person over fifteen [1]; unlike the earlier poll taxes of 1377 and 1379, this was not graduated by wealth, so the poor paid the same as the rich [1]. Feature 2: The Poll Tax was deeply resented because one shilling could represent a week's wages for a poor peasant family [1]; many communities refused to pay or hid people from tax collectors, leading to government commissioners being sent to enforce collection in 1381 [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one long-term cause of the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a specific long-term cause (serfdom, the Statute of Labourers 1351, the Black Death's economic legacy creating a gap between peasants' practical value and legal status) and explains it in depth with precise factual knowledge, showing how it built up over decades before 1381. Secure: Identifies a cause and explains it with relevant factual support. Developing: States a cause with limited explanation. Emerging: Vague reference without specific factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the failing French Wars for the people of England in the late 1370s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains a consequence in depth — e.g. the fiscal pressure of the wars produced three Poll Taxes between 1377 and 1381; the flat-rate 1380 Poll Tax was especially resented; or the loss of territories won at Brétigny damaged the Crown's prestige and made further taxation seem unjustifiable. Secure: Explains a consequence with relevant factual support. Developing: States a consequence with limited development. Emerging: Vague point without factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Poll Tax of 1380 to the outbreak of the Peasants' Revolt.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains significance at the time (flat rate was deeply unfair; commissioners sent to collect unpaid amounts acted as the immediate trigger in Essex and Kent; combined with long-term resentment to produce revolt) and longer-term (Poll Tax abandoned after the revolt; became a symbol of royal overreach; the name 'Poll Tax' remained politically toxic for centuries). Precise factual knowledge throughout. Secure: Explains significance at the time with some longer-term reference. Developing: Describes the Poll Tax without clearly explaining significance. Emerging: Limited knowledge; significance not addressed.

practice_questions.text:
'The most important cause of the Peasants' Revolt was the Poll Tax of 1380.' How far do you agree?
Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with precise factual knowledge. Agrees: the Poll Tax was the immediate trigger; its flat rate was uniquely unjust; the arrival of commissioners to collect unpaid amounts was the detonating event in Essex and Kent. Disagrees: deeper causes were equally important — the Statute of Labourers (1351), continued serfdom despite the Black Death's economic changes, John Ball's decade of radical preaching, and the cost of failed wars all fed into 1381; without them the Poll Tax alone might not have produced revolt. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Makes points for and against with evidence. Developing: Describes causes without evaluating the interpretation. Emerging: Simple response; no judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: What was John Ball's central argument about serfdom?
options: That serfs should pay higher tithes to the Church
That God made all people equal and serfdom was therefore contrary to divine law
That only the king had the right to free serfs
That serfs should be armed to defend England against France

knowledge_checks.q: What made the 1380 Poll Tax particularly resented compared to earlier poll taxes?
options: It was collected by foreign tax collectors
It was a flat rate of one shilling per head regardless of wealth
It was the first poll tax ever levied in England
It funded the Church rather than the French wars

knowledge_checks.q: The Peasants' Revolt began in _____ and Kent, counties where the Statute of Labourers had been especially aggressively enforced.
John Ball's rhyme — 'When _____ delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?' — argued that the social order was not God-given.
Match each person to their role in the events leading to the Peasants' Revolt:
right: Reversed English territorial gains after Brétigny, increasing war costs
Radical priest who preached equality and serfdom's illegitimacy
Led the Kentish rebels and negotiated with Richard II at Mile End

flashcard_questions.q: What was John Ball's famous rhyme about social equality?
flashcard_questions.a: 'When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?'

What flat rate did the 1380 Poll Tax impose?
flashcard_questions.a: One shilling per head for every person over fifteen, regardless of wealth.

flashcard_questions.q: Why was the 1380 Poll Tax more unfair than earlier ones?
flashcard_questions.a: It was not graduated by wealth — the poor paid the same as the rich.
Followers of John Wyclif's theological ideas, who criticised Church wealth and papal authority in late fourteenth-century England.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did the French Wars create pressure for higher taxation in the late 1370s?
flashcard_questions.a: The gains of Brétigny were being reversed by France, making campaigns costly without decisive results.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did the Peasants' Revolt begin in Essex and Kent specifically?
flashcard_questions.a: Both counties had experienced aggressive Statute of Labourers enforcement and had relatively prosperous communities able to organise resistance.
The leader of the Kentish rebels in 1381, who led the march on London and negotiated with Richard II.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Statute of Labourers passed, and what did it try to do?
flashcard_questions.a: 1351; it tried to fix wages at pre-Black Death levels and prevent workers from moving between employers.

flashcard_questions.q: Where was John Ball at the start of the Peasants' Revolt?
flashcard_questions.a: In prison; he was freed by the rebels.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the immediate trigger for the Peasants' Revolt in 1381?
flashcard_questions.a: Government commissioners sent to collect the unpaid 1380 Poll Tax in Essex and Kent.

glossary_terms.definition: The legal condition of unfree peasants who were bound to a lord's manor and owed labour and other dues; deeply resented after the Black Death had demonstrated peasants' economic value.

A radical priest and preacher whose sermons challenged the social order by arguing that God made all men equal and that serfdom was contrary to divine law; a key intellectual figure behind the Peasants' Revolt.

Followers of John Wyclif's theological ideas in late fourteenth-century England, who criticised Church wealth and the authority of the Pope; sometimes associated with early challenges to the social order.
A flat-rate tax levied on every person above a specified age, regardless of wealth; the 1380 Poll Tax was deeply resented because the poor paid the same as the rich.
The leader of the Kentish rebels in 1381, whose charismatic leadership gave the Peasants' Revolt its organisational focus; he was killed at the Smithfield meeting with Richard II.

hero_image_caption: Medieval peasants gathering, representing the discontent that drove the revolt of 1381.
